endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Permitted Uses and Disclosures: Must be limited to defined functions (e.g., data hosting, analytics).

endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: (a) requested by a health care provider with the consent of the Utah user;

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: If protected health information (PHI) is involved, organizations should execute appropriate Business Associate Agreements, apply the “minimum necessary” standard, and maintain safeguards commensurate with risk.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: AI developers may enter into legal arrangements (e.g., business associate agreements) that bring them under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Vendors should be asked whether they guarantee that data will not be used to predict sensitive health information or identity information outside the context of the AI solution.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether BAAs or DUAs that list permitted and prohibited AI data uses, require minimum necessary data, and bar re-identification reduce vendor secondary use or re-identification of patient data. Five sources endorse the practice, and two of them, one framework and one statute, use mandatory language.

perspectives.view: The map lists zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Certainty therefore rests at no direct evidence. The recommendation draws on frameworks, guidance, and one statute. These sources reflect expert consensus, but they do not show that contract terms change vendor behavior or reduce harm to patients.

CHAI playbooks state that permitted uses must be limited to defined functions, and Utah HB 452 uses mandatory language tied to provider request with user consent. RUAIH guidance says organizations should execute BAAs and apply minimum necessary. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide says vendors should be asked about predicting identity information, and the augmented intelligence principles treat BAAs as optional.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared AI vendor agreements that contain enumerated use limits, minimum necessary terms, and re-identification bans against generic agreements. Useful studies would measure audited vendor secondary use, data volumes transferred, retention beyond contract terms, and re-identification incidents. They would also test whether contract language is monitored and enforced after signing.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet tell whether these contract terms protect those patients to the same degree as other patients.
